vignette:
Mariana sits in the armchair with her back to the wall. She chose this seat herself, two sessions ago, scanning the room first the way she scans a crime scene – methodically, checking for exits, for blind spots. She is a detective with the city’s Major Crimes Unit, a rank she earned through fifteen years of relentless competence. At thirty-nine, she is sharp, respected, and never caught off guard. Or so she tells herself.

When she speaks, it is in clipped sentences, as if every word is evidence she must weigh before releasing it. But today her voice wavers for a second. She is telling me about a case she worked last week – a domestic disturbance that turned into a homicide. The victim was a woman, thirty-four, strangled by her partner in front of their two children. Mariana’s jaw tightens as she describes the scene: the overturned coffee table, the smeared blood on the linoleum, the children’s toys scattered like small, silent witnesses.

“I can’t get the sound out of my head,” she says. “The little boy. He kept saying, ‘Mami, get up, Mami, get up.’”

She looks down at her hands. She does not cry. She rarely cries. Instead, she feels a familiar pressure in her chest, the kind she learned to carry as a child and has never put down.

She was six years old, living in a small apartment in the Bronx, when her father came home drunk for the last time before leaving them for good. She remembers the sharp click of the lock, the way her mother’s face went still. Mariana was supposed to be asleep, but she had learned to stay awake, to listen for the change in his footsteps. That night, she crept to the door of her bedroom and saw him shove her mother against the refrigerator. The sound of her mother’s back hitting the metal. The muffled sobs. Mariana stood frozen, her hand over her own mouth, because if she made a sound, he might turn on her. She learned then that love was a trap, that safety was an illusion.

In the years since, she has built her life around control. She became a detective because she needed to make sense of violence, to chase it down and handcuff it. She is good at it. Her partner, Carlos, says she has a gift for reading people. What he does not know is that she reads everyone the same way: for danger signs, for the flicker of a raised voice, the subtle clench of a fist.

At home, she is with Diego, a high school history teacher. They have been together for six years. He is patient and kind, and she loves him, but she is always waiting. Waiting for the shift. When he raises his voice in excitement over a documentary, her body goes cold. When he reaches for her suddenly in the kitchen, she flinches before she can stop herself. He has learned to announce his movements. “I’m coming up behind you,” he will say. She hates that he has to.

Sleep is a ruined thing. She wakes three or four times a night, heart pounding, checking the locks, listening for a floorboard that never creaks. She has not gone a full week without a nightmare since she was a child. In the worst ones, she is six again, but this time she cannot move. The door is open, and her father is walking toward her, and she can only watch.

At work, she is relentless. She volunteers for the hardest cases, the ones that keep her away from home for days. When she comes back, she is hollowed out, unable to tell Diego what she has seen. He knows not to ask. They have a rhythm now that keeps her safe: distance, silence, the careful management of anything that might crack her open.

She does not think of herself as a victim. She has never told a partner about her childhood. When the department offered crisis counseling after a particularly brutal case, she declined. She does not want to be seen as fragile. She wants to keep doing the job that gives her a reason to be vigilant, a reason to be ready. But lately, the edges are fraying. The nightmares come every night. She has started checking the locks four times instead of three. She jumped at a car backfiring in the parking lot last month and had to sit down for five minutes before her hands stopped trembling.

That is why she is here, sitting with her back to the wall, telling me about the little boy who could not wake his mother. She does not want to feel anything. But the feeling comes anyway, pushing up from her chest like a hand reaching through dark water. She swallows it down. She is an expert at that.
